title: My Clinic — Clinical Governance: Quality, Patient Safety & Risk
description: Quality standard, the six International Patient Safety Goals, risk scoring, incident types and the 24-hour reporting rule.

metadata.description: Quality standard, the six International Patient Safety Goals, risk scoring, incident types and the 24-hour reporting rule.

objectives.description: Classify quality measures as structure, process or outcome and order the FOCUS-PDCA cycle.
Apply the six International Patient Safety Goals, including the two-identifier rule.
Score a risk on the 5×5 matrix and choose an appropriate response.
Distinguish critical incidents, adverse events and near misses within a just culture.
Report an incident through the correct channel within 24 hours.

screens.title: Clinical governance
screens.subtitle: Quality, patient safety and risk
screens.notes: Companion: Noor, char-noor-welcome, L1 portrait card bottom-right (alt: Noor, the safety liaison, smiling and waving in welcome.). Speaker: Noor.
screens.narration_text: Noor: Hello, I'm Noor, a senior nurse and patient-safety liaison. Welcome to clinical governance: how My Clinic protects patients every day. You'll link daily decisions to quality, safety, risk and reporting.

screens.title: The quality standard
screens.body_html:
SECTION 1 OF 7

“Doing the right things right — the first time, and every time.” ⚠ PENDING B1
screens.media_alt: Decorative Caring value tile with a white line icon; the value name is text.
screens.narration_text: Noor: Clinical governance connects the way a service is organised with the way care is delivered and the results patients experience. It asks teams to use reliable information, learn from problems and improve practice over time. Keep one question in mind: what helps the next patient receive safe, consistent care? The standard is a daily way of working, not a slogan.

screens.title: Speak up safely
screens.prompt_html:
Have you ever noticed something unsafe at work and not said anything?

Anonymous response handling ⚠ PENDING NEW-01
screens.reflection_html: This reflection is not scored. Continue to the practice screens.
screens.notes: Companion: Noor, char-noor-listening, right column beside the poll, never over the options (alt: Noor, the safety liaison, holding a tablet and listening.). Speaker: Noor.
screens.narration_text: Noor: Most of us have stayed quiet about something unsafe at least once. I have. Speaking up gets easier every time. Answer honestly, or pass.

screens.title: How quality is measured
screens.image_alt: Diagram linking structure, processes and outcomes, with a separate improvement-cycle callout.
screens.prompt_html:
Collect valid, reliable data that reflects actual performance.

FOCUS-PDCA improvement cycle: exact step names ⚠ PENDING B11.

feedback.correct_html: The diagram links structure, processes and outcomes; use reliable data to understand performance.
feedback.incorrect_html: Review each labelled stage and the relationship shown by the arrows.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Start with structure: the resources and setting available to provide care. Processes describe what the team does and how consistently it is done. Outcomes describe the results for patients. The three layers connect, but they answer different questions. Reliable, valid data helps a team understand actual performance rather than rely on impressions. The improvement cycle shown here connects measurement to action; confirm its approved step names before production. The arrow shows how measurement supports improvement over time.

screens.title: Classify the measures
screens.prompt_html: Place each illustrative measure in Structure, Process or Outcome. These are practice examples, not My Clinic performance results.

items.text_html: Percentage of patients checked with two identifiers ⚠ PENDING B4
HbA1c control in a diabetes programme

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Resources are structure, actions are process, and patient results are outcomes. These examples are practice items, not local performance data.
feedback.incorrect_html: Look at what each measure observes: available resources, a care activity, or a result for patients.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Classify each measure as resources, actions or patient results. Apply the definitions from the previous screen before checking.

screens.title: FOCUS-PDCA: order the steps
screens.prompt_html: Arrange the FOCUS-PDCA steps in order. ⚠ PENDING B11: confirm exact labels before release.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. FOCUS leads into Plan–Do–Check–Act; improvement continues as a cycle. ⚠ PENDING B11: confirm exact approved terms.
feedback.incorrect_html: Rebuild the order from the organisation-approved FOCUS-PDCA model. Treat improvement as a repeating cycle.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Arrange the nine steps in order and show how the last begins the next cycle. Don't skip a step.

screens.title: Six patient-safety goals
screens.image_alt: Six icon panels represent the six patient-safety goals; panel names and practices are also available as text.
screens.prompt_html: Open all six goals. Draft practice wording requires policy confirmation ⚠ PENDING B3.

regions.label_html:
Goal 1 — Identification ⚠ PENDING B3

Use two approved identifiers. Exact rule ⚠ PENDING B4.
regions.feedback_html: Identification helps match care to the intended patient. Confirm the approved identifiers before release.

regions.label_html:
Goal 2 — Communication ⚠ PENDING B3

Verify verbal/telephone orders, report critical results and use structured handover.
regions.feedback_html: Communication practices reduce ambiguity at handover and when orders or results are shared.

regions.label_html:
Goal 3 — High-alert medicines ⚠ PENDING B3

Draft mentions a red label and independent double-check.
regions.feedback_html: Use the facility’s approved high-alert medication process; confirm details before production.

regions.label_html:
Goal 4 — Safe procedures ⚠ PENDING B3

Draft practices include verification, site marking, time-out and sign-out.
regions.feedback_html: Procedure safeguards must follow the current facility policy and approved terminology.

regions.label_html:
Goal 5 — Hand hygiene ⚠ PENDING B10

Five moments: before patient contact, before a clean procedure, after body-fluid exposure risk, after patient contact, after surroundings.
regions.feedback_html: Use the facility poster wording for each moment before release.

regions.label_html:
Goal 6 — Fall prevention ⚠ PENDING B5

Draft source mentions a high-risk identifier band; confirm its colour and use.
regions.feedback_html: Confirm the falls-policy identifier before naming or illustrating it.

feedback.correct_html: All six goal panels are open. Use the confirmed facility wording before release.
feedback.incorrect_html: Open the remaining goal panels to complete the exploration.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Patient safety is supported by six linked goals, not one reminder. Each goal names an area where teams can reduce avoidable risk. Open every pillar and read the practice paired with it. The exact wording, numbering and several details still need policy confirmation, so these descriptions are marked for review before release. Use the approved facility language once it is confirmed. The exercise is meant to help you connect a goal with a daily action.

screens.title: Which patient?
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-noor-avatar-concern}}Noor · Safety liaison

Two fictional patients named Mohammed Al-Harbi are waiting for blood tests. Fictional training record numbers: 100245 and 100871. Confirm identity before care continues.

nodes.image_alt: Two blank wristbands; fictional names and record numbers are shown as accessible HTML text.
nodes.prompt_html: One patient is ready for a blood test. How do you confirm you have the right record?

choices.text_html: Ask the full name and compare the medical record number on the wristband with the request.
choices.feedback_html: Correct for the draft. The source plan names full name and medical record number. Confirm the facility rule before release. ⚠ PENDING B4

choices.text_html: Use the room number to choose the record.
choices.feedback_html: A room number is not one of the two identifiers named in the draft. Confirm the official rule. ⚠ PENDING B4
The source says age must not be used as an identifier. Confirm the facility’s approved wording. ⚠ PENDING B4

nodes.image_alt: Two fictional wristbands share one name and show different fictional record numbers.
nodes.prompt_html: The names match exactly. What should happen next?

choices.text_html: Pause and use the additional identifier specified by policy: date of birth or national ID. ⚠ PENDING B4
choices.feedback_html: The Phase 2 draft names date of birth or national ID when names match. Use only the confirmed local rule. ⚠ PENDING B4

choices.text_html: Use age or room number as a tie-breaker.
choices.feedback_html: Age and location are not safe tie-breakers. Follow the confirmed identifier policy. ⚠ PENDING B4

choices.text_html: Guess based on who looks familiar.
choices.feedback_html: Familiarity does not verify identity. Stop and use the additional identifier allowed by policy. ⚠ PENDING B4

nodes.image_alt: Two blank wristbands; the fictional name and record numbers are shown as accessible HTML text.
nodes.prompt_html: A colleague says, “It’s the older one.” What do you do?

choices.text_html: Pause the draw, explain that age is not an identifier, and re-verify using approved identifiers. ⚠ PENDING B4
choices.feedback_html: Correct for the draft. Do not proceed on age or assumption; use the confirmed identifiers. ⚠ PENDING B4

choices.text_html: Proceed because the colleague knows the patient.
choices.feedback_html: Familiarity does not replace the identifier check. Pause and verify before care continues. ⚠ PENDING B4
A bystander cannot resolve an identity mismatch. Follow the approved identifier process. ⚠ PENDING B4

feedback.correct_html: You have practised pausing and verifying identity. Use the confirmed identifiers and same-name rule.
feedback.incorrect_html: Revisit the approved identifier policy and the reasons each shortcut is unsafe.

screens.notes: Companion: Noor L5 scenario avatar above the situation — char-noor-avatar-concern on intro, char-noor-avatar-happy / char-noor-avatar-concern after each choice. Speaker: Noor (honest story, companions.md §1).
screens.narration_text: Noor: I once nearly drew blood from the wrong Mr Al-Harbi. The wristband stopped me. Now two fictional patients share one full name. Decide what you check, and what you do if both names match.

feedback.incorrect_html: Compare each practice with the purpose of the goal label. Several details remain pending policy review.

screens.title: Five moments
screens.prompt_html: Arrange the five moments in the order shown in the approved hand-hygiene guidance. ⚠ PENDING B10.

items.text_html: Before touching a patient ⚠ PENDING B10
Before a clean/aseptic procedure ⚠ PENDING B10
After body-fluid exposure risk ⚠ PENDING B10
After touching a patient ⚠ PENDING B10
After touching patient surroundings ⚠ PENDING B10

feedback.correct_html: Correct. The five moments cover before care, before an aseptic task, after exposure risk, after care and after the patient’s surroundings. Verify exact poster wording. ⚠ PENDING B10
feedback.incorrect_html: Think about before patient contact, before a procedure, and after contact or exposure. Confirm the facility poster wording.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Order the five hand-hygiene moments around patient contact and the care task; include every stage without skipping one.

screens.title: Risk-management lifecycle

items.text_html: Report exposure in the risk register

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Identify and assess the risk, put controls in place, monitor them, then report exposure in the risk register.
feedback.incorrect_html: Monitoring follows assessment and management; reporting records exposure in the risk register.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Arrange the risk-management lifecycle from the first step through reporting, using the agreed labels. It's a sequence, not a score.

screens.title: Score a risk
screens.intro_html: Hypothetical case only—not a My Clinic event. Expired stock is found twice in a fictional clinic refrigerator. Risk lifecycle: identify → assess → manage → monitor → report.

steps.rationale_html: For this hypothetical exercise, the possible consequence is a product that may not work as intended.
This is a teaching input, not a measured local incident rate.
The source defines the numeric score as impact multiplied by likelihood on a 1-to-5 scale.

steps.action_html: Look up score 12 on the corporate matrix.
steps.rationale_html: Use the confirmed band name and threshold; do not infer them. ⚠ PENDING B6.
steps.artifact_caption: Corporate risk matrix; exact bands and colours pending B6.

steps.action_html: Compare the draft response labels: Reduce · Transfer · Accept · Avoid. ⚠ PENDING B7
steps.rationale_html: Use only the response terms and approval conditions confirmed by the Risk Manager. ⚠ PENDING B7

screens.self_explanation_prompt_html: What control could reduce impact or likelihood in this hypothetical case? This is an unscored reflection.
screens.notes: Companion: Dr. Omar, char-omar-thinking, L3 right column half-body (alt: Dr. Omar, the family physician, with his hand at his chin, thinking through the risk score.). Speaker: Omar.
screens.narration_text: Omar: Let's score one together. It's a made-up case: expired items turn up twice this month in a clinic fridge. Impact first. A patient could get a vaccine that doesn't work, so we call impact four. It has already happened twice, so likelihood is three. Four times three gives twelve. Honestly, the number alone doesn't tell you what to do. The band for twelve comes from our corporate matrix, which Risk is still confirming. Then choose a response that lowers the risk, such as a weekly checklist with a second check. Treat those controls as teaching examples until Quality and Risk approve them.

screens.title: Calculate the risk score

feedback.correct_html: 5 × 2 = 10. Read the band from the approved matrix. ⚠ PENDING B6.
feedback.incorrect_html: Multiply impact by likelihood; do not guess the band. The approved range is pending B6.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Calculate the score from the impact and likelihood values, then use the confirmed matrix to supply its band.

screens.title: Choose the risk response
screens.prompt_html: Match each risk response with the action it describes. ⚠ PENDING B7.

pairs.right_html: Add a second-check control to lower likelihood.
Transfer financial exposure to an insurer.
Leadership reviews and approves continued exposure.
Do not start the risk-creating activity.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Responses control, transfer, formally accept or avoid exposure. Confirm policy labels and conditions. ⚠ PENDING B7
feedback.incorrect_html: Re-read each action: lower exposure, transfer it, approve living with it, or stop the activity.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Match each risk response with the action it describes. Use the policy-approved terms once confirmed, then check your reasoning.

screens.title: The safety iceberg
screens.image_alt: Iceberg with three labelled positions for critical or sentinel events, adverse events and near misses; exact terms are pending B8.
screens.prompt_html: Event names and definitions are draft pending incident-policy confirmation. ⚠ PENDING B8

labels.text: Critical incident / sentinel event ⚠ PENDING B8
Adverse event — harm reached a person ⚠ PENDING B8
Near miss — caught before harm ⚠ PENDING B8

feedback.correct_html: The diagram separates the draft event categories by position; final names and definitions remain pending B8.
feedback.incorrect_html: Review the three labelled layers and confirm their definitions with the policy owner.

screens.notes: Companion: Dr. Omar tip card bottom-left — char-omar-avatar-neutral, label "Omar's tip": Caught it before it reached the patient? Report it anyway. It costs nothing and protects the next person. Speaker: Omar.
screens.narration_text: Omar: Picture an iceberg. At the tip are the most serious events, the ones everyone hears about. Just below the waterline are events that reach a patient and cause harm. The biggest part sits deep down: near misses, caught before any harm. Here's what helped me. I treat every near miss as a free lesson about a weak process. The exact terms and examples are still being confirmed by Risk.

screens.title: Classify the event
screens.prompt_html: Classify each fictional event by what happened and whether harm reached a person. ⚠ PENDING B8.

items.text_html: Patient falls and needs stitches ⚠ PENDING B8
Wrong drug given; mild rash ⚠ PENDING B8
Wrong drug prepared but caught before giving ⚠ PENDING B8
Lab sample has wrong name; caught at lab desk ⚠ PENDING B8

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Consider the event’s consequence and whether it was caught before reaching the person. Final definitions remain pending B8.
feedback.incorrect_html: Ask what happened, whether harm reached a person, and whether the failure was caught in time. Confirm the terms with policy.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Classify each fictional event by what happened and whether harm reached the person. The labels remain subject to policy confirmation.

screens.title: A just culture?
screens.prompt_html: If you report a near miss you caused, you will be disciplined. ⚠ PENDING B8

feedback.correct_html: Correct for the draft. The source describes an open, non-punitive culture and says reports are not used to criticise staff. Confirm policy limits and wording. ⚠ PENDING B8
feedback.incorrect_html: The source’s draft message is non-punitive reporting. Verify how the current policy defines accountability. ⚠ PENDING B8

screens.narration_text: Noor: Consider the statement carefully. Decide whether it reflects the open, non-punitive culture described in the source, pending policy confirmation.

screens.title: Report an event

blocks.html:
What to report

Clinical: medication errors, falls. Non-clinical: system downtime, equipment failure, lab issues, fire hazards and security breaches.

When

Within 24 hours in the source draft. ⚠ PENDING B9 / D8

Where and what follows

Digital intranet form or email in the source draft. The system grades, escalates and analyses reports. Channel confirmation ⚠ PENDING B9.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Reportable events include clinical concerns and problems affecting facilities, equipment, laboratories, fire safety or security. The source describes a digital report through the intranet or by email, followed by review, grading and escalation. The exact reporting channel and time limit require confirmation. The current draft shows a 24-hour window. Do not rely on it until the policy owner confirms it and aligns the wording with Module 03. Add factual details and immediate actions, not assumptions.

screens.title: End-of-shift near miss
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-noor-avatar-neutral}}Noor · Safety liaison

Fictional 19:00 shift-end scenario: earlier, you caught a colleague about to give insulin to the wrong patient. No one was harmed.

nodes.prompt_html: No patient was harmed. What should happen next?

choices.text_html: Report the near miss through the approved process. ⚠ PENDING B8
choices.feedback_html: Best choice in the draft. Reporting a near miss can reveal a weak process before harm occurs. Confirm the event policy. ⚠ PENDING B8

choices.text_html: Do not report because no harm occurred.
choices.feedback_html: The source describes reporting near misses; confirm the final definition and process with policy. ⚠ PENDING B8

choices.text_html: Wait to see whether the same problem happens again.
choices.feedback_html: Waiting leaves the possible system weakness unreported. Use the confirmed process. ⚠ PENDING B8

choices.text_html: Within the confirmed reporting window; the draft says within 24 hours. ⚠ PENDING B9/D8
choices.feedback_html: Best choice in the draft. The current draft says within 24 hours; use the final policy window once confirmed. ⚠ PENDING B9/D8

choices.text_html: Next week, when the shift is quieter.
choices.feedback_html: Delay may exceed the approved window. Submit within the confirmed time limit. ⚠ PENDING B9/D8
The draft includes near misses; confirm reportability in the current policy. ⚠ PENDING B8/B9

choices.text_html: Use the confirmed digital channel or email and record factual details, not blame. ⚠ PENDING B9
choices.feedback_html: Best choice in the draft. Use the approved channel and record facts and immediate actions. Confirm the channel before release. ⚠ PENDING B9

choices.text_html: Write assumptions about the colleague’s intent.
choices.feedback_html: Record observable facts and immediate actions, not assumptions or blame. Use the approved channel. ⚠ PENDING B9

feedback.correct_html: Review the confirmed reporting workflow and submit facts through the approved channel.
feedback.incorrect_html: Revisit the approved incident-reporting procedure and the current time window.

screens.narration_text: Noor: A fictional near miss happened near the end of a tiring shift. No one was harmed, but the risk was real. Choose what to do next, then decide when and where the report belongs under the confirmed policy.
